summary: Defines managed objects for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units, the hardware that connects an Ethernet device to its cable, so they can be managed with SNMP. It was replaced by RFC 3636.

eli5.summary: The piece that plugs a computer into an Ethernet cable can be checked remotely. This memo lists the things a manager can look at.

questions: how do you monitor ethernet interface hardware
subtitle: SNMP objects for managing Ethernet network interface hardware.

tldr.problem: Ethernet devices have hardware components (MAUs) that connect them to cables, but there was no standard way to monitor and manage these components remotely via SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a MIB (Management Information Base) with SNMP objects for monitoring the status, configuration, and performance of IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs), the hardware adapters that connect devices to Ethernet cables.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can now use SNMP to check on Ethernet interface hardware health without physical access. It was replaced by RFC 3636.

today: RFC 1515 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 3636, which provides managed objects for Ethernet-like interfaces. Modern management systems use the updated RFC 3636 for Ethernet and MAU monitoring, though the basic concepts defined here remain foundational to SNMP network management.

sections.title: Why Manage MAUs
sections.content:
An IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Unit (MAU) is the hardware that physically connects a device to an Ethernet cable or network segment. MAUs come in different types depending on the cable medium: thick coaxial cable (10BASE5), thin coaxial (10BASE2), twisted-pair copper (10BASE-T), fiber-optic (FOIRL, 10BaseFP, 10BaseFB, 10BaseFL), broadband (10BROAD36), or no attachment (AUI).

Each MAU needs to be monitored for faults, configuration changes, and operational status. This RFC defines SNMP objects so that a network management station can query MAU status and receive alerts when problems occur, without requiring a network administrator to physically visit the equipment.
sections.eli5: The piece that plugs your device into the network needs to work properly. This document describes how to check on it and get warnings if something goes wrong.

sections.title: Structure: Repeater MAUs and Interface MAUs
sections.content:
The MIB defines two categories of MAUs: repeater MAUs and interface MAUs. A repeater MAU is attached to a port on an IEEE 802.3 repeater (a network device that retransmits signals to extend a collision domain). An interface MAU is attached directly to a device interface, as in a router, switch, or workstation.

The MIB is organized into three main groups: the Repeater MAU Basic Group, the Interface MAU Basic Group, and the Broadband MAU Basic Group (for 10BROAD36 MAUs only). Each group contains configuration, status, and control objects. A repeater MAU can also define internal MAUs embedded in a device, such as when a repeater includes a management port.
sections.eli5: MAUs come in two flavors: ones that attach to repeaters (network hubs) and ones that attach directly to device ports. The document has a section for each type and one for a special type called broadband.

sections.title: Managed Objects for MAU Status and Configuration
sections.content:
For each MAU, the MIB defines objects that track the MAU type (using an object identifier from a list of standard types), the operational status, and whether the media (cable) is available. The RFC captures two important counters: mediaAvailableStateExits, which counts transitions when the media becomes unavailable, and jabberingStateEnters, which counts instances when the MAU enters a jabbering state (continuous incorrect transmission that corrupts the network).

Repeater MAUs and interface MAUs are indexed differently. A repeater MAU is identified by its group index, port index, and MAU index within that port. An interface MAU is indexed using the interface index from MIB-II, the standard MIB, allowing integration with other Ethernet interface monitoring.
sections.eli5: For each MAU, you can see what type it is, whether it is working, whether the cable is plugged in, and how many times it has had problems like jabber (broken transmission).

sections.title: Integration with Other SNMP MIBs
sections.content:
This MAU MIB is designed to extend the standard MIB-II and the IEEE 802.3 Repeater MIB. Any agent implementing the MAU MIB must also implement the 'system' group from MIB-II, which provides basic system information like name, description, and uptime.

For interface MAUs, the agent must implement the 'interfaces' group from MIB-II and should implement the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB, which provides higher-level interface statistics. For repeater MAUs, the agent must implement the 802.3 Repeater MIB. This hierarchical structure allows management software to navigate from high-level interface statistics down to detailed MAU-level diagnostics.
sections.eli5: MAU objects fit into the standard SNMP structure, so a management station that understands standard SNMP can find and query them without special knowledge.

sections.title: Notifications and Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines SNMP traps (notifications) that a MAU can send to alert a management station of important events. These include transitions in media availability and entries into a jabber state. A network administrator can configure SNMP to automatically receive these alerts at a monitoring station, allowing proactive detection of cable failures or hardware faults.

The MIB includes identifiers for all standard 802.3 MAU types, including unshielded twisted pair (10BaseT), various fiber options, coaxial variants, and broadband. New MAU types can be added as technology evolves, and management stations can determine the capability of each interface based on its MAU type.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the MAU can send an alarm message to the management station. The RFC also lists all the known types of MAUs so managers know what type of adapter they are dealing with.
